t: The Greeks worshipped many gods, led by the twelve Olympians under Zeus, together with heroes, nymphs and local powers, through sacrifice, prayer, festivals and oracles, with no sacred book and no single priesthood to define belief.
Religion was woven into the life of every city: its temples, such as the Parthenon, its festivals, such as the Panathenaia and the Olympic Games, and its drama, born in the festivals of Dionysus.
Banned by the Christian emperors in the 390s, it left myths, told by Homer, Hesiod and the tragedians, that became one of the foundations of Western art and literature.
dyk: The ancient Olympic Games were a religious festival of Zeus: athletes swore an oath before a statue of the god, and a hundred oxen were sacrificed at his great altar in the middle of the festival.
ev: Tablets in Linear B at Knossos and Pylos record offerings to Zeus, Hera, Poseidon and Dionysus
The first Olympic Games are held in honour of Zeus, by tradition
Homer’s epics and Hesiod’s Theogony give the gods their classic form
Pheidias’s gold and ivory statue of Athena is dedicated in the Parthenon
Socrates is condemned to death in Athens for impiety
The emperor Theodosius bans all pagan sacrifice and worship
The last ancient Olympic Games are held, by tradition
Justinian forbids pagans to teach; the Platonic school of Athens closes

f.origin: The Aegean world: gods such as Zeus, Hera, Poseidon and Dionysus are named on Mycenaean tablets of the 14th and 13th centuries BCE
f.founder: None; its myths took their classic form in the poems of Homer and Hesiod around 700 BCE
f.scriptures: No sacred book: the epics of Homer, Hesiod’s Theogony, the Homeric Hymns and the sacred laws and calendars of each city
f.followers: None as an ancient tradition: the Christian emperors banned its sacrifices in the 390s; a modern revival was recognised in Greece in 2017
